Poulson Chapter 1 Lisbeth Longfuck goes to Hull Farm.
Bear Hunter, the big, shaggy old dogger Hull Farm, sat on the stone step in front of the house, looking soably around the spacious door yard.
It was a clear cold winter's day toward the beginning of spring, and the sunshine brightly over the glittering snow.
In spite of the bright sunshine, however, Bear Hunter would have liked to be indoors much better than out.
If he sensed responsibility had permitted, for his paws ached with a cold, and he had to keep holding them up one after another from the stone slab to keep from getting the claw ache.
Bear Hunter did not wish to risk that, because claw ache is very painful as every northern dog knows.
But to leave his post at Watchman was not to be thought of just now, for the pigs and the goats were out today.
At this moment they were very busy with their separate affairs and behaving very well.

The pigs over at the sunny side of the door yards, scratching themselves against the corner of the cowhouse, and the goats gnawing back from the big heap of pine branches that had been laid near the sheep barn for their special use.

They looked as if they thought of nothing but their scratching and gnawing, but Bear Hunter knew well from previous experience that no sooner would he go into the house than both pigs and goats would come rushing over to the doorway and do all the mischief they could.

That big goat crook horn, the new one who had come to the farm last autumn, and whom Bear Hunter had not yet bought under discipline, had already strayed in a round about ways to the very corner of the farmhouse and was looking at Bear Hunter in a self -important manner, as if she did not fear him in the least.
She was really an intolerable creature that goat crook horn, but just let her dare.
Bear Hunter felt he must sit on the cold doorstep for some time longer at any rate.
He could not stop the road occasionally as if to see whether anyone was coming, so that the pigs and goats might not think they had the whole of his attention.
He had just turned his head leisurely towards the narrow road that came in down crosswise over the slope from the upper farms when what in the world was that?
Something was coming, a funny little rolly pole or something.
What a pity thought Bear Hunter that his sight was growing so poor.
Had any way he had better give the people at the house warning.
So he gave several deep echoing barks.
The goats sprang together in a clump and rose there is, the pigs stopped and the very midst of their scratching to listen.
That Bear Hunter was holding great respect could easily be seen.
He still remains sitting on the doorstep staring up the road.
Never in his life had he seen such a thing as that now approaching.
Perhaps after all it was nothing worth giving warning about.
He would take a turn up the road and look at it at the whole nearer.
So arching his bushy tail into a handsome curve and putting on his most good human expression he sought it off.
Yes it must be a human being although you would not think so.
It began to look very much like Katrina the Finn as they called her who came to the farm every winter.
But it could not be Katrina it was all together too little.
It wore a long wide skirt and from under the skirt protruded the tips of two big shoes covered with grey wool and stocking feet from which the legs had been cut off.
Above the skirt there was a round bundle of clothes with a nethered chal tied rounded and from this protruded two stumps with red mittens on.
Perched on top of it all was a smaller shape muffled in a smaller nethered chal.
That of course must be the head.
Carried at the back was a huge bundle tied up in the dark cloth and in front hung a pretty wooden pile painted red.
Really bare hunter had the stand still in the gaze.
The strange figure in the meantime had become aware of him and it also came to a stand still as if in a dilemma.
At that bare hunter walked over to the father side of the road and took his station there trying to look indifferent for he did not wish to cause any fright.
The strange figure then made its way carefully forward again drawing gradually closer and closer to its own side of the road.
As it came near at a bare hunter the figure turned itself round by degrees until when directly opposite to him it walked along quite sidewise.

Then it was that bare hunter got a peep through a little opening in the upper shore and there he saw the tip of a tiny turned up red nose then a red mouth that was drawn down a little at the corners as if ready for crying and then a pair of big blue eyes that were fastened upon him with a look of terror.
Poo, it was nothing all but a little girl well bundled up against the cold.
Bare hunter did not know her but white a bit he thought he had seen that pile before at any rate it would be absurd to try to frighten this queer little creature.
His style began to wag in voluntarily as he walked across the road to take a sniff at the pile.
The little girl did not understand his action at once stepping back in alarm she caught her heels in her long frok and down she tumbled by the side of the road.
Bare hunter darted off instantly but after running a short distance toward the health he stopped and looked at her again making his eyes as gentle as he could and waging his tail energetically.
With bare hunter that waging of the town and hearty good natured after.
Then a little girl understood she got up smart and jogged slowly after him.
Bare hunter trotted leisurely ahead looking back at her from time to time.
He knew now that she had an errand at high old farm and that he was therefore in duty bound to help her.
Thus it was that Lith the longfot of Peer Out Castle made her entrance into her farm.
Peer Out Castle was purged tie above the upper farms when a crag that jutted out for a barren ridge just under a mountain peak called the Big Hammer.

The real name of the little farm was new ridge and Peer Out Castle was only a nickname given to it by a joker because there was so fine an outlook from it and because it bore no resemblance whatever to a castle.
The Royal Lands belonged to this castle consists of a little plot of cold -evaded soil.
I a bit have made our land here and there and some Heather patches where tiny blue debris bushes and small mountain crane replans grew luxurably.
The castle's outbuildings were a Shelby Cowhouse and a pig's thigh.
The Cowhouse was built against the steep hillside with three walls of loosely built stone and its two stalls were dug half their length into the hill.
The tiny pig's thigh was built in the same fashion.
As for the castle itself that was a very very small turf -roofed cabin lying out on the jutting crag in the middle of the rocky ridge.

It had only one small window with tiny pains of glass that looked out over the valley and yet in whatever path of the surrounding country one might be by looking in that direction and looking high enough one could always see that little castle with its single window peering out like a watchful eye over the landscape.
Since the castle from which this was longfot came was no more magnificent than this, it may easily be understood that she was no disguised princess but only a poor little girl.
Coming to her farm from the first time was for her like visiting an estate that was in very true thru oil and beside she had come on an important grown up errand.
She was taking her mother's place and visiting her as a spinning woman.
This was mother whose name was Randy had worked hard for the last four years to get food for herself and her children up at Peerhead Castle.
Before that the family had been in very comfortable circumstances but the father had died leaving the mother with a castle one car and a car of two children.
The children were Jacob at that time about six years old and Lisbeth a couple of years younger.

Life was often a hard struggle for the mother but they had it anyway a house over their heads and they could get wood without having to go very far for it since the forest lay almost within a stone's throne.
In the summer Randy managed to dig up her tonny plot of ground after a fashion so that she could harvest a few potatoes in a little grain.
By cutting grass and stripping off birch leaves she had thus far managed each year to give blueros their cow enough to eat and where there is a cow there was always food.

In the winter she spun linen and wool for the women on the farm's far and near but as she had lived at her farm as a servant before she was married it was natural that most of her spinnings should be for Kirsty Hill.
In such ways had Randy been able to care for her family.
Meanwhile Jacob now ten years old had grown big enough to earn his own living.
In the spring before the last a message had come from Nordrum Farm that a boy was needed to look after the flocks and Jacob had a one supply then been accepted.
He and Lisbeth had often knelt on the long wooden bench under the little window at pier out castle and gazed upon the different farms choosing which they would work on when they were big enough.
Jacob had always chosen Nordrum Farm, possibly because he had heard Farmer Nordrum spoken of as the big man of the community.
While Lisbeth had always thought it would be pleasant there at Hill Farm because it was owned by a woman.
When Autumn came Farmer Nordrum had concluded that he would have a use for a boy such as Jacob during the winter also and so Jacob had stayed on.
This last Christmas however he had gone home for the whole day and had taken within a Christmas present for his sister from a little girl at Nordrum.
The presents was a grey woolen frock a very nice one.
Jacob had grown extremely pleasant and full of fun while at Nordrum Lisbeth thought.
When she tried the frock on that reached way down to the ground before and behind he called her Lisbeth Longfork and Lisbeth Longfork she had remained for that day.
After Christmas times had been somewhat harder at pier out castle.
But he Ross who generally gave milk the whole year round had become dry and would not give milk for several months.
She was to have a calf in the early summer.
During that last few weeks there had been not enough even for Randy and Lisbeth's coffee.
To go to Svihagen the nearest farm for milk was no short trip and milk was scarce there too as Randy well knew.
Besides she could not spare the time to go she had the finished spinning Kirsty Hills wool.
When she once got that off her hands they could have fed him up for their coffee and other good things be signed.
What a relief it would be when that time came.
So Randy worked steadily at her spinning.
This was being now big enough to help in cutting the wool.
For a week she spun almost without ceasing, scarcely taking time for meals for drinking a good deal of strong back coffee.
Not till very late one evening with Kirsty Hills wool all spun and ready.
By that time Randy was far from well.

Whether or not her illness was caused as she thought by drinking so much black coffee, certain ideas that when Kirsty Hills wool was all spun, Randy felt a tightness in her chest and when she got up the next morning and tried to get ready to go to her with the spinning she was seized with such a sudden business that she had to go back to bed again.
She was too weak for anything else.
Now it was the custom in Norway for the spinning woman to take back to the different farms the wool she had spun.
And for the farmer's wife to praise her work treated her something good to wait and drink to pay her and then give her directions about the way the next spinning was to be done.
All this Randy would have to give up for the present.
There was no help for it but she wondered how it would do to send Lisbeth to her farm in her stead.
The little girl would find her wise safely Randy was sure that Randy had never has yet taken to that farm because it was so far off.
Payment for the spinning was to be in eatables as well as money and Lisbeth could bring her in part of what was due.
Then though they might lack many things their drop of coffee would have cream in it as coffee ought to have.
The remainder of the payment and the directions for next spinning Randy herself could get when she was better.
If only she could be sure that Lisbeth would behave properly or not act like a changeling a troll child.
Lisbeth eagerly promised that if her mother would allow it a go she would behave exactly as a spinning woman should.
She would really and she remembered perfectly well just how everything was done that time she had gone with her mother to one of the nearer farms.
So Lisbeth put on her longfork which was only used for the very best and her mother wrapped her snuggling the two shores.
Then the bundle of yarn was long over her back.
The pair was hung in front many directions were given to her about the road and off she started.
And that is the way Lisbeth longfork happened to come tolding out the bear hunter to her farm on that clear cold winter's day toward the beginning of spring.
